newsitem.title: GERMANY: German "wise man" urges quick tax reform.
newsitem.headline: German "wise man" urges quick tax reform.

text.p: Germany must reach a quick deal to pass planned tax reforms if it is to boost investment and win the battle against record post-war unemployment, a senior government economic advisor urged on Thursday.

Plans that Bonn has been discussing with opposition Social Democrats (SPD) proposals would encourage companies to invest in projects that create jobs in Germany, Rolf Peffekoven, a member of the "five wise men" advisory panel, said.
"If the reforms that are on the table were to pass, the investment situation would improve," he told ZDF public TV.
Germany's corporate tax system requires broad reform in order to convince companies to use their profits to help boost the country's ailing economy, he said.
Although corporate giants like Deutsche Bank AG, Veba AG and BMW AG all announced profit rises in 1996 on Wednesday, many German companies were still directing investments abroad, Peffekoven said.
Government plans to cut corporate taxes -- which if passed without being diluted would reduce the main rate to 35 percent by 1999 from 47 percent now -- would help investment.
"What would be better for a company than to invest with high write-off conditions and to pay lower taxes on profits later?" he said. "Something must happen on this front."

The SPD pulled out of cross-party tax talks with the coalition in a recent row over coal subsidies, and party leader Oskar Lafontaine has demanded a face-to-face meeting with Chancellor Helmut Kohl to restart the negotiating process.

Kohl has rejected that condition and coalition leaders have in recent days played down prospects for an early deal, saying that, with the SPD able to block tax measures in parliament's upper hose, they would end up having to do a deal later in the lengthy parliamentary mediation process.

The coalition has already brought its 1998 tax bill into parliament, and plans to launch legislation for 1999 -- which contains the lion's share of 30 billion marks in income and corporate tax cuts -- some time after the Easter break.
